title: Sprachtest Englisch v2
desc: Lese-/Textverständnis, Vokabeltest, Verben und Orthografie & Grammatik – 20 Aufgaben je Testlauf, 10 Minuten. 50 eigenständige Testläufe (1.000 Aufgaben insgesamt); jeder Testlauf deckt alle 4 Aufgabentypen ab.
intro: Vier Aufgabentypen im Wechsel: (1) Lese-/Textverständnis – zu einem kurzen Text mehrere Aussagen als „correct" oder „not correct" beurteilen; (2) Vokabeltest – eine Lücke im Satz mit dem passenden Wort füllen; (3) Verben – eine Lücke mit der richtigen Form des in Klammern angegebenen Verbs füllen (alle vier Optionen sind Formen desselben Verbs, geprüft wird also Tempus, Aspekt und Diathese, nicht die Wortwahl); (4) Orthografie & Grammatik – die korrekt verbesserte Version eines fehlerhaften Satzes auswählen. Jeder Testlauf deckt alle vier Typen ab (6 + 5 + 5 + 4 = 20 Aufgaben) in 10 Minuten.

run1.label: Testlauf 1 – 20 Aufgaben · 10 Min
run1.note: Teil 1 Lese-/Textverständnis (6 Aufgaben zu einem Textabschnitt), Teil 2 Vokabeltest (5 Aufgaben), Teil 3 Verben (5 Aufgaben), Teil 4 Orthografie & Grammatik (4 Aufgaben). 10 Minuten für alle 20 Aufgaben.

items.q: The course treats every negotiation as a fixed pie to be divided.
items.e: Nicht richtig – Text sagt das Gegenteil: Optionen sollen „value for both sides“ schaffen, „rather than merely dividing a fixed pie“.
items.passage:
Negotiation is a core skill for anyone representing an organisation in dealings with partners, suppliers or authorities. Our two-day workshop trains participants to prepare systematically, to distinguish between positions and underlying interests, and to develop options that create value for both sides rather than merely dividing a fixed pie.

Role-plays based on realistic case studies allow participants to practise techniques such as anchoring, active listening and the strategic use of silence. Special attention is given to negotiating across cultures, where directness, the pace of discussion and the role of hierarchy can differ considerably. By the end of the course, participants will be able to plan a negotiation strategy, recognise common tactics used by counterparts, and close agreements that are both fair and sustainable.

items.q: The workshop ignores cultural differences in negotiation style.
items.e: Nicht richtig – Text sagt das Gegenteil: „Special attention is given to negotiating across cultures“.

items.q: The minister has brushed ____ the accusations, saying he is not in the least worried.
items.e: „to brush aside“ = etwas (eine Anschuldigung, Kritik) beiseiteschieben, nicht ernst nehmen.

items.q: After weeks of talks, the two delegations finally reached an ____ on the border dispute.
items.e: „to reach an agreement“ = eine Einigung erzielen.

items.q: The prime minister flatly ____ any wrongdoing during the press conference.
items.e: „to deny wrongdoing“ = ein Fehlverhalten bestreiten.

items.q: The opposition has ____ the government of covering up the scandal.
items.e: „to accuse somebody of something“ = jemanden einer Sache beschuldigen.

items.q: Following the vote of no confidence, the chancellor was forced to step ____.
items.e: „to step down“ = zurücktreten, sein Amt niederlegen.

items.q: A vicious separatist campaign ____ (launch) by rebels has been raging since 1984.
items.e: Verlangt ist „launched" — Past Simple von „launch". Die übrigen Optionen sind Formen desselben Verbs, passen aber nicht in die Zeit-/Diathesenlogik des Satzes (launch, launches, launching).

items.q: In recent months the group ____ (step) up its attacks considerably.
items.e: Verlangt ist die zusammengesetzte Form „has stepped" von „step"; die übrigen Optionen sind einfache Formen desselben Verbs und tragen die geforderte Zeit-/Diathesenstufe nicht.

items.q: Few of the provinces ____ (dominate) by the minority are ethnically homogeneous.
items.e: Verlangt ist „dominated" — Past Simple von „dominate". Die übrigen Optionen sind Formen desselben Verbs, passen aber nicht in die Zeit-/Diathesenlogik des Satzes (dominate, dominates, dominating).

items.q: In television debates and across the blogosphere, support for the idea ____ (grow) steadily.
items.e: Verlangt ist die zusammengesetzte Form „is growing" von „grow"; die übrigen Optionen sind einfache Formen desselben Verbs und tragen die geforderte Zeit-/Diathesenstufe nicht.

items.q: The ruling party currently ____ (plan) to deploy a new professional force along the border.
items.e: Verlangt ist „plans" — 3. Person Singular Präsens von „plan". Die übrigen Optionen sind Formen desselben Verbs, passen aber nicht in die Zeit-/Diathesenlogik des Satzes (plan, planned, planning).

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „Never in my career have I witnessed such a breach of protocol as this."
o: Never in my career have I witnessed so a breach of protocol as this.
Never in my career have I witnessed such a breach of protocol as this.
Never in my career have I witnessed such breach of protocol as this.
Never in my career I have witnessed such a breach of protocol as this.
items.e: Zwei Punkte zugleich: „Never" am Satzanfang erzwingt die Inversion („have I witnessed"), und vor einem zählbaren Substantiv im Singular steht „such a", nicht „so a" oder artikelloses „such".

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „We received less complaints after the update.“
o: We received fewer complaints after the update.
We receive fewer complaints after the update.
We received least complaints after the update.
We received less complaint after the update.
items.e: "complaints" ist zählbar: "fewer complaints".

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „We need to do a decision by Friday.“
o: We need making a decision by Friday.
We need to do a decisions by Friday.
We need do a decision by Friday.
We need to make a decision by Friday.
items.e: "make a decision" ist die feste Kollokation, nicht "do a decision".

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „They may to attend the ceremony next week.“
o: They may to attending the ceremony next week.
They may attend the ceremony next week.
They may to attends the ceremony next week.
They may attended the ceremony next week.
items.e: Nach "may" folgt der bloße Infinitiv: "may attend".

run2.note: Teil 1 Lese-/Textverständnis (6 Aufgaben zu einem Textabschnitt), Teil 2 Vokabeltest (5 Aufgaben), Teil 3 Verben (5 Aufgaben), Teil 4 Orthografie & Grammatik (4 Aufgaben). 10 Minuten für alle 20 Aufgaben.

items.q: The workshop is aimed only at delegates, not secretariat staff.
items.e: Text nennt ausdrücklich „delegates and secretariat staff“ als Zielgruppe.
items.passage:
Chairing a multilateral meeting well is a distinct skill from simply having the most senior title in the room. Our one-day workshop trains delegates and secretariat staff to manage speaking lists fairly, keep discussion within agreed time limits without appearing high-handed, and steer a room of divergent interests towards a text that enough delegations can live with, even if none of them love it.

Particular attention is given to the moment when consensus stalls: participants practise techniques such as suspending a contentious paragraph for informal consultations, proposing bridging language on the spot, and reading the room to judge when a vote, rather than further debate, is the more honest outcome. Role-plays are drawn from real committee transcripts, with names and positions altered. By the end of the course, participants will be able to draft a realistic agenda, manage interventions from the floor without losing control of the room, and recognise the difference between a genuine objection and a delaying tactic.

items.q: Participants practise suspending a contentious paragraph for informal consultations.
items.e: Text: „suspending a contentious paragraph for informal consultations“ wird als Technik genannt.

items.q: The ceasefire was declared unilaterally but never took full ____.
items.e: „to take effect“ = wirksam werden, in Kraft treten.

items.q: Negotiators hope to hammer ____ a compromise before the deadline expires.
items.e: „to hammer out a compromise“ = einen Kompromiss mühsam aushandeln.

items.q: The two countries have agreed to a bilateral ____ aimed at reducing tension along the border.
items.e: „ceasefire“ = Waffenstillstand.

items.q: The ambassador was summoned to explain the remarks made by her ____.
items.e: Kontext: die Botschafterin vertritt ihre Regierung ('government') im Ausland.

items.q: The treaty's most controversial provisions were widely ____ by legal scholars.
items.e: „to criticise a provision“ = eine Bestimmung/Klausel kritisieren.

items.q: Thousands of villagers ____ (imprison) during the unrest of the 1990s.
items.e: Verlangt ist die zusammengesetzte Form „were imprisoned" von „imprison"; die übrigen Optionen sind einfache Formen desselben Verbs und tragen die geforderte Zeit-/Diathesenstufe nicht.

items.q: Some fighters simply ____ (disappear) without a trace after the crackdown.
items.e: Verlangt ist „disappeared" — Past Simple von „disappear". Die übrigen Optionen sind Formen desselben Verbs, passen aber nicht in die Zeit-/Diathesenlogik des Satzes (disappear, disappears, disappearing).

items.q: The allied forces are ____ (provide) intelligence to their partners in the region.
items.e: Verlaufsform (Present Continuous): „are" + **Partizip Präsens** — „are providing". Die drei anderen Optionen scheiden aus: „provides" = finite Präsensform der 3. Person Singular — nach einem Hilfsverb ausgeschlossen; „provide" = Grundform (Infinitiv) — kann in dieser Position nicht stehen; „provided" = Partizip II — ergäbe Perfekt bzw. Passiv statt der Verlaufsform.

items.q: The party ____ (call) its programme a bold new opening at the time.
items.e: Verlangt ist „called" — Past Simple von „call". Die übrigen Optionen sind Formen desselben Verbs, passen aber nicht in die Zeit-/Diathesenlogik des Satzes (call, calls, calling).

items.q: The authorities have been ____ (accuse) local activists of ties to the banned organisation.
items.e: Present Perfect Continuous: „have been" + **Partizip Präsens** — „have been accusing". Die drei anderen Optionen scheiden aus: „accused" = Partizip II — ergäbe Perfekt bzw. Passiv statt der Verlaufsform; „accuse" = Grundform (Infinitiv) — kann in dieser Position nicht stehen; „accuses" = finite Präsensform der 3. Person Singular — nach einem Hilfsverb ausgeschlossen.

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „Each department submit its own budget request.“
o: Each department submits its own budget request.
Each department submitted its own budget request.
Each department submit's its own budget request.
Each department submitting its own budget request.
items.e: "Each" + Einzahl-Subjekt verlangt "-s": "submits".

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „There is little we can do at this stage, is there?"
o: There is little we can do at this stage, is it?
There is little we can do at this stage, isn't there?
There is little we can do at this stage, doesn't it?
There is little we can do at this stage, is there?
items.e: „little" ist bereits negativ, das Frageanhängsel bleibt daher bejaht; bei „there is" wird „there" wiederaufgenommen, nicht „it".

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „He is good in negotiating difficult contracts.“
o: He is good at negotiating difficult contracts.
He is well at negotiating difficult contracts.
He is good on negotiating difficult contracts.
He good at negotiating difficult contracts.
items.e: "good at doing something" ist die feste Präposition, nicht "good in".

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „She checks always her emails before the meeting.“
o: She checks her always emails before the meeting.
She always checks her emails before the meeting.
She always checking her emails before the meeting.
She checks always her email before the meeting.
items.e: Häufigkeitsadverb vor dem Vollverb: "always checks".

items.q: Hostile questions are said to be avoided entirely during the seminar.
items.e: Nicht richtig – Text sagt das Gegenteil: es wird trainiert, „hostile questions“ ruhig zu beantworten, nicht sie zu vermeiden.
items.passage:
Confident public speaking is essential for anyone who must brief superiors, address the media or represent an institution before an audience. This one-day seminar combines short theoretical input with extensive individual practice, all recorded on video for immediate feedback.

Participants learn how to structure a presentation around a clear message, how to use voice, pause and gesture deliberately, and how to handle nervousness before and during a talk. A further focus lies on answering difficult or hostile questions calmly, without losing the thread of the argument. Because every participant delivers at least three short presentations during the day, the group size is deliberately kept small, with no more than eight people per course, so that each person receives detailed, individual feedback.

items.q: Presentations are recorded on video for feedback.
items.e: Richtig – Text: „all recorded on video for immediate feedback“.

items.q: The president's popularity has slipped amid growing public ____ over the economy.
items.e: „public discontent“ = öffentliche Unzufriedenheit.

items.q: Talks between the two sides broke ____ after just three hours.
items.e: „talks broke down“ = Gespräche scheiterten/wurden abgebrochen.

items.q: The government has come under fire for its handling of the ____.
items.e: „to come under fire for“ = wegen etwas scharf kritisiert werden.

items.q: The reform was passed despite fierce ____ from within the ruling party itself.
items.e: „fierce opposition“ = heftiger Widerstand.

items.q: Diplomats are working around the clock to broker a ____ before the summit ends.
items.e: „to broker a deal“ = einen Deal/eine Einigung vermitteln.

items.q: One senior official has ____ (suggest) that citizens should be treated equally regardless of origin.
items.e: Present Perfect: „has" + **Partizip II** — „has suggested". Die drei anderen Optionen scheiden aus: „suggesting" = Partizip Präsens — ergäbe eine Verlaufsform, die der Satz nicht verlangt; „suggest" = Grundform (Infinitiv) — kann in dieser Position nicht stehen; „suggests" = finite Präsensform der 3. Person Singular — nach einem Hilfsverb ausgeschlossen.

items.q: Despite years in custody, the leader to this day still ____ (retain) the loyalty of his followers.
items.e: Verlangt ist „retains" — 3. Person Singular Präsens von „retain". Die übrigen Optionen sind Formen desselben Verbs, passen aber nicht in die Zeit-/Diathesenlogik des Satzes (retain, retained, retaining).

items.q: Secret ____ (talk) with the imprisoned leader have reportedly been going on for months.
items.e: Verlangt ist „talks" — 3. Person Singular Präsens von „talk". Die übrigen Optionen sind Formen desselben Verbs, passen aber nicht in die Zeit-/Diathesenlogik des Satzes (talk, talked, talking).

items.q: As the prime minister ____ (know) only too well today, abandoning reform now would strengthen his opponents.
items.e: Verlangt ist „knows" — 3. Person Singular Präsens von „know". Die übrigen Optionen sind Formen desselben Verbs, passen aber nicht in die Zeit-/Diathesenlogik des Satzes (know, knew, known).

items.q: As an old proverb ____ (say), every stick has two ends.
items.e: Verlangt ist „says" — 3. Person Singular Präsens von „say". Die übrigen Optionen sind Formen desselben Verbs, passen aber nicht in die Zeit-/Diathesenlogik des Satzes (say, said, saying).

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „He is working for this company since three years.“
o: He has worked for this company since three years.
He works for this company since three years.
He is working for this company for three years.
He has worked for this company for three years.
items.e: Present Perfect + "for" bei Zeitdauer, nicht Present Continuous + "since".

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „He didn't give no explanation for the decision.“
o: He didn't gave no explanation for the decision.
He didn't give none explanation for the decision.
He gave no explanation not for the decision.
He didn't give any explanation for the decision.
items.e: Keine doppelte Verneinung: "didn't give any explanation".

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „He shall to present the findings at the summit.“
o: He shall to presenting the findings at the summit.
He shall present the findings at the summit.
He shall to presents the findings at the summit.
He shall presented the findings at the summit.
items.e: Nach "shall" folgt der bloße Infinitiv: "shall present".

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „She is a honest and reliable colleague.“
o: She is a honestly and reliable colleague.
She are an honest and reliable colleague.
She is an honest and reliably colleague.
She is an honest and reliable colleague.

items.q: The programme is aimed at senior staff.
items.e: Text: „coaching programme for junior staff“, nicht für Senior-Personal.
items.passage:
Public speaking rarely feels risky when the audience is friendly and the questions are predictable. Our two-day coaching programme for junior staff focuses instead on the moments that actually determine credibility: an unscripted question from the floor, a hostile follow-up, or a request to summarise a complex position in a single sentence. Participants are filmed delivering short statements and then review the footage with a coach, focusing on pace, filler words and the instinct to over-explain when nervous.

A recurring exercise asks participants to answer the same difficult question three times, each time in fewer words, until only the essential point remains. The programme deliberately avoids scripted rhetoric in favour of a small number of structural habits — stating the conclusion first, bridging back to it after any digression — that hold up even under pressure. By the end, participants will be able to handle an unscripted question without visibly losing composure and to compress a complex answer without distorting it.

items.q: The minister's resignation came as no ____ to seasoned observers.
items.e: „to come as no surprise“ = keine Überraschung sein.

items.q: The new sanctions are intended to ____ pressure on the regime.
items.e: „to increase pressure on somebody“ = Druck auf jemanden erhöhen.

items.q: The scandal has cast a long ____ over the upcoming election.
items.e: „to cast a shadow over something“ = etwas überschatten.

items.q: Both leaders agreed to set ____ their differences for the sake of the alliance.
items.e: „to set aside differences“ = Differenzen zurückstellen.

items.q: The proposal was quietly ____ after facing overwhelming criticism.
items.e: „to shelve a proposal“ = einen Vorschlag auf Eis legen.

items.q: He ____ (brush) aside the accusations, insisting he was untroubled by them.
items.e: Verlangt ist „brushed" — Past Simple von „brush". Die übrigen Optionen sind Formen desselben Verbs, passen aber nicht in die Zeit-/Diathesenlogik des Satzes (brush, brushes, brushing).

items.q: The minister ____ (deny) any wrongdoing when questioned by reporters.
items.e: Verlangt ist „denied" — Past Simple von „deny". Die übrigen Optionen sind Formen desselben Verbs, passen aber nicht in die Zeit-/Diathesenlogik des Satzes (deny, denies, denying).

items.q: An Italian newspaper has ____ (allege) that the politician knew about the affair for months.
items.e: Present Perfect: „has" + **Partizip II** — „has alleged". Die drei anderen Optionen scheiden aus: „allege" = Grundform (Infinitiv) — kann in dieser Position nicht stehen; „alleging" = Partizip Präsens — ergäbe eine Verlaufsform, die der Satz nicht verlangt; „alleges" = finite Präsensform der 3. Person Singular — nach einem Hilfsverb ausgeschlossen.

items.q: Before their first meeting, he ____ (give) her a considerable sum of money, she said.
items.e: Verlangt ist „gave" — Past Simple von „give". Die übrigen Optionen sind Formen desselben Verbs, passen aber nicht in die Zeit-/Diathesenlogik des Satzes (give, gives, given).

items.q: The prime minister was said to have ____ (offer) her a rent-free flat on his estate.
items.e: Perfekt-Infinitiv: „to have" + **Partizip II** — „to have offered". Die drei anderen Optionen scheiden aus: „offers" = finite Präsensform der 3. Person Singular — nach einem Hilfsverb ausgeschlossen; „offering" = Partizip Präsens — ergäbe eine Verlaufsform, die der Satz nicht verlangt; „offer" = Grundform (Infinitiv) — kann in dieser Position nicht stehen.

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „He asked me did I finish the report.“
o: He asked me did I finish the report.
He asked me whether I had finished the report.
He asked me if did I finish the report.
He asked me had I finish the report.
items.e: Ja/Nein-Fragen in indirekter Rede mit "whether/if" einleiten, keine Inversion: "whether I had finished".

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „Do you know what time does the meeting start?“
o: Do you knows what time the meeting starts?
Do you know what time the meeting start?
Do you know what time the meeting starts?
Do you know what time does the meeting starts?
items.e: Eingebettete Frage ohne "does": "what time the meeting starts".

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „We review usually the budget at the end of the quarter.“
o: We review usually the budgets at the end of the quarter.
We usually review the budget at the end of the quarter.
We review the usually budget at the end of the quarter.
We usually reviewing the budget at the end of the quarter.
items.e: Häufigkeitsadverb vor dem Vollverb: "usually review".

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „She is studying medicine since four years.“
o: She is studying medicine for four years.
She has studied medicine since four years.
She has been studying medicine for four years.
She studies medicine since four years.
items.e: Andauernde Handlung mit Zeitdauer: Present Perfect Continuous + "for".

items.q: Public Wi-Fi networks are not mentioned in the course.
items.e: Nicht richtig – Text sagt das Gegenteil: „safe practices for...public Wi-Fi networks“ wird genannt.
items.passage:
Most successful cyber-attacks on organisations begin not with a technical flaw but with a single careless click. This half-day course raises awareness among staff of all levels about phishing e-mails, fraudulent phone calls and the manipulation techniques known as social engineering.

Using real, anonymised examples, participants learn to recognise suspicious messages, to verify unusual requests through a second channel, and to report incidents immediately rather than trying to fix them alone. The course also covers safe practices for mobile devices, public Wi-Fi networks and password management, including the use of a password manager. Given how quickly attack methods evolve, we recommend refreshing this training every twelve months, and offer a short online update course for returning participants.

items.q: Without citing any supporting evidence, the report ____ that the ministry had known about the risks for years.
items.e: „alleges“ = behauptet unbewiesen; „without citing any supporting evidence“ schließt das belegbasierte „concludes“ aus.

items.e: „to be at odds over something“ = uneins sein.

items.e: „to prevent something from happening“ = etwas verhindern.

items.q: The wording of the statement was chosen carefully to avoid ____ either side.
items.e: „to antagonise“ = gegen sich aufbringen, verärgern.

items.q: The same version was said to have been ____ (give) to police the following year.
items.e: Perfekt-Infinitiv im Passiv: „to have been" + **Partizip II** — „to have been given". Die drei anderen Optionen scheiden aus: „give" = Grundform (Infinitiv) — kann in dieser Position nicht stehen; „gives" = finite Präsensform der 3. Person Singular — nach einem Hilfsverb ausgeschlossen; „gave" = Past Simple — eine finite Form; die Position verlangt das Partizip II.

items.q: That incident ____ (put) an end to the connection between the two of them.
items.e: Verlangt ist „put" — Infinitiv/Grundform von „put". Die übrigen Optionen sind Formen desselben Verbs, passen aber nicht in die Zeit-/Diathesenlogik des Satzes (puts, putting, has put).

items.q: The centre-left newspaper has ____ (publish) an extract from the leaked testimony.

items.q: Mobile telephone records ____ (show) that she had visited the mansion on several occasions.
items.e: Verlangt ist „showed" — Past Simple von „show". Die übrigen Optionen sind Formen desselben Verbs, passen aber nicht in die Zeit-/Diathesenlogik des Satzes (show, shows, shown).

items.q: Her longest stay ____ (cover) a period during which a foreign head of state was also present.
items.e: Verlangt ist „covered" — Past Simple von „cover". Die übrigen Optionen sind Formen desselben Verbs, passen aber nicht in die Zeit-/Diathesenlogik des Satzes (cover, covers, covering).

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „We have been partners for the year 2015.“
o: We have been partners from the year 2015.
items.e: Für einen Startzeitpunkt ("since"), nicht eine Dauer mit "for" bei einem Jahr, das als Startpunkt gemeint ist.

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „The new model is more faster than the old one.“
o: The new model is most faster than the old one.
The new model is more fast than the old one.
The new model is fastest than the old one.
The new model is faster than the old one.
items.e: Kein doppeltes Komparativ: "faster", nicht "more faster".

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „She has been appointed to a European coordinating body for one year."
o: She has been appointed to an European coordinating body for one year.
She has been appointed to a European coordinating body for an one year.
She has been appointed to a European coordinating body for one year.
She has been appointed to the European coordinating body for a one year.
items.e: „European" beginnt phonetisch mit dem Konsonantenlaut /j/, daher „a European"; „one year" steht ohne Artikel.

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „Is this the report which were sent to headquarters?“
o: Is this the report which were send to headquarters?
Are this the report which was sent to headquarters?
Is this the reports which were sent to headquarters?
Is this the report which was sent to headquarters?
items.e: Einzahl-Subjekt "the report" verlangt "was", nicht "were".

items.q: The briefing focuses only on clearly illegal situations.
items.e: Text sagt das Gegenteil: der Fokus liegt auf Grauzonen, nicht auf eindeutig legalen/illegalen Fällen.
items.passage:
Anti-corruption compliance is too often reduced to a signature on an annual declaration. Our half-day briefing for managers takes a different approach, working through concrete grey areas: a supplier's invitation to a lavish conference, a request to expedite a permit through a well-connected intermediary, a gift that is modest in itself but arrives just before a contract decision.

Participants examine each scenario against the organisation's own thresholds for gifts and hospitality and practise the short, factual escalation memo expected when a situation is ambiguous rather than clearly compliant or clearly wrong. The briefing is explicit that the goal is not to make every manager a lawyer, but to make hesitation itself the trigger for asking compliance rather than deciding alone. A closing session addresses facilitation payments specifically, since staff frequently assume — incorrectly — that small payments to speed up routine administrative processes are treated differently from other forms of bribery under the organisation's policy.

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „I asked her why doesn't she attend the summit.“
o: I asked her why doesn't she attend the summit.
I asked her why she didn't attend the summit.
I asked her why not she attended the summit.
I asked her why she not attended the summit.
items.e: Kein Hilfsverb in eingebetteten Fragen; Aussagesatz-Wortstellung: "why she didn't attend".

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „She had already went home when we called.“
o: She had already gone home when we called.
She has already gone home when we called.
She had already going home when we called.
She had already go home when we called.
items.e: Past Perfect: "had gone" (Partizip Perfekt von go), nicht "went" (Simple Past).

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „They are living in this house since 2015.“

They have lived in this house since 2015.

They live in this house since the year 2015.
items.e: Present Perfect (Continuous) + "since" bei einem Startzeitpunkt einer andauernden Handlung.

Organisations that draw on the full range of their employees' backgrounds and perspectives make better decisions and are more resilient to change. Our diversity and inclusion programme begins by helping participants recognise unconscious bias in recruitment, promotion and everyday interactions.

items.q: The training only covers matching client names, not beneficial ownership.
items.e: Text nennt beides: Namensabgleich UND „identifying beneficial ownership behind layered corporate structures“.
items.passage:
Sanctions regimes change quickly, and a screening process that was adequate two years ago can quietly fall behind. Our one-day training for compliance officers at financial institutions covers the practical mechanics of due diligence: matching client names against consolidated sanctions lists while accounting for transliteration variants, identifying beneficial ownership behind layered corporate structures, and recognising the red flags that distinguish a legitimate complex transaction from one designed to obscure its true parties.

Case studies are drawn from publicly available enforcement actions, anonymised where necessary. Particular emphasis is placed on false positives: participants learn that an overly aggressive matching algorithm which flags every plausible namesake creates its own risk, since staff under pressure to clear a backlog begin approving flagged transactions without genuine review. The training closes with a session on documenting the rationale for a screening decision, since regulators consistently focus less on whether a decision was correct in hindsight than on whether it was reasoned and recorded at the time.

items.q: An afternoon is dedicated to risk management.
items.e: Richtig – Text: „A full afternoon is dedicated to risk management“.
items.passage:
Delivering projects on time and within budget requires more than good intentions; it requires a systematic method. This three-day course introduces both classic, plan-driven project management and agile approaches, and helps participants decide which is appropriate for a given task.

Topics include defining a realistic scope, building a work breakdown structure, estimating effort, and managing stakeholders who may have conflicting expectations. A full afternoon is dedicated to risk management: identifying what could go wrong, estimating likelihood and impact, and preparing responses in advance rather than reacting under pressure. Participants complete the course by applying the tools to a project of their own choosing and presenting a short plan to the group, which receives structured peer feedback.

items.q: The briefing recommends addressing the interpreter directly rather than the counterpart.
items.e: Text sagt das Gegenteil: man solle der Versuchung widerstehen, „to address the interpreter directly rather than the counterpart“.
items.passage:
Working through an interpreter changes the dynamics of a negotiation in ways that are easy to underestimate. Our half-day briefing prepares officials for exactly this: speaking in short, complete units of meaning rather than long, looping sentences that strain an interpreter's memory; avoiding idioms and culturally specific references that resist accurate rendering; and resisting the temptation to address the interpreter directly rather than the counterpart.

Participants practise pausing naturally at the end of a thought rather than mid-sentence, and learn to notice when an interpreter's hesitation signals not a language problem but a genuinely ambiguous statement that needs to be rephrased at the source. The briefing also covers the practical courtesy of providing interpreters with terminology lists and background documents well in advance, since even highly skilled interpreters perform markedly worse when specialist vocabulary is sprung on them without warning. By the end, participants will be able to structure their own delivery to make an interpreter's task easier rather than harder.

items.q: Participants are taught to avoid idioms and culturally specific references.
items.e: Text: „avoiding idioms and culturally specific references that resist accurate rendering“.

Participants practise pausing naturally at the end of a thought rather than mid-sentence, and learn to notice when an interpreter's hesitation signals not a language problem but a genuinely ambiguous statement that needs to be rephrased at the source. The briefing also covers the practical courtesy of providing interpreters with terminology lists and background documents well in advance, since even highly skilled interpreters perform markedly worse when specialist vocabulary is sprung on them without warning. By the end, participants will be able to structure their own delivery to make an interpreter's task easier rather than harder.

items.q: The trainers claim time management is mainly a collection of tricks.
items.e: Nicht richtig – Text sagt das Gegenteil: „a matter of decisions about priorities, not a collection of tricks“.
items.passage:
Many professionals feel busy all day yet finish it without making progress on what matters most. This one-day workshop addresses that gap between activity and achievement.

Participants learn to distinguish urgent tasks from important ones, to plan their week around a small number of priorities rather than an ever-growing list, and to protect blocks of undisturbed time for demanding work. Practical sessions cover techniques for handling e-mail more efficiently, for saying no to low-value requests without damaging relationships, and for delegating tasks appropriately. The trainers emphasise that time management is ultimately a matter of decisions about priorities, not a collection of tricks, and that no technique will help someone who has not first clarified their actual goals.

items.q: The workshop treats brevity and vagueness as the same thing.
items.e: Text sagt ausdrücklich das Gegenteil: „brevity is not the same as vagueness“.
items.passage:
Drafting a policy brief sounds like a writing exercise until a minister has ninety seconds to read it before walking into a meeting. Our one-day workshop trains staff to compress a complex issue into a single page without hollowing it out: a short framing of the problem, two or three clearly labelled options with their trade-offs stated rather than implied, and a recommendation that does not hide behind vague language such as "further consideration is warranted".

Participants draft, exchange and critique each other's briefs under time pressure, with particular attention paid to executive summaries that quietly contradict the body of the document they are meant to summarise. A recurring theme is that brevity is not the same as vagueness: a one-page brief can still commit to a clear position, and a shorter document that avoids a real recommendation is not actually shorter, since the reader still has to do the thinking the brief was meant to do for them. The workshop closes with a session on adapting the same underlying analysis for readers at different levels of seniority.

items.q: Case studies are drawn from real cross-border projects.

items.passage:
Working across borders means working across assumptions that are rarely made explicit. This training helps staff who cooperate with international partners understand how communication styles, attitudes to time, and ways of giving feedback vary between cultures, and, more importantly, how to adapt without abandoning one's own professional standards.

Through case studies drawn from real cross-border projects, participants examine misunderstandings that arose from differing expectations about punctuality, hierarchy and directness of speech. items.q: The seminar is designed for finance specialists rather than programme managers.
items.e: Text: „one-day seminar for programme managers“, nicht für Finanzspezialisten.
items.passage:
Public budgeting is often taught as a set of spreadsheet rules, which is precisely why so many finance briefings for non-specialists fail to stick. Our one-day seminar for programme managers instead starts from the questions auditors actually ask: why a budget line grew between two fiscal years, what happens to unspent funds at year end, and how a virement between budget lines is authorised and documented.

Participants work through a simplified but realistic departmental budget, identifying which variances need a one-line explanation and which require a formal justification memo. Considerable time is spent on the distinction between under-spending that reflects genuine efficiency and under-spending that signals a programme was never properly resourced to begin with — auditors treat the two very differently, even though both look identical on a spreadsheet. The seminar ends with a practical session on preparing for an audit interview, including how to answer a question honestly without volunteering unrelated problems that were not actually asked about.

items.q: Feedback covers body language, tone and clarity.
items.e: Richtig – Text: „frank feedback on body language, tone and clarity“.
items.passage:
A single poorly handled interview can undo months of careful communication work. This media training prepares spokespeople and executives for interviews with journalists, whether in front of a camera, on the radio, or in writing.

Participants first learn to define three key messages before any interview and to return to them regardless of the question asked, a technique known as bridging. Simulated interviews, conducted by a former journalist and recorded on camera, allow participants to experience the pressure of a real interview and to receive frank feedback on body language, tone and clarity. The course also addresses how to handle hostile or repeated questions calmly and how to correct a factual error made live without appearing evasive.

items.q: The briefing assumes staff already know these basics and skips them.
items.e: Text sagt das Gegenteil: es behandelt genau das, „that most offices assume everyone already knows but few were ever actually taught“.
items.passage:
Records management rarely feels urgent until the day a file cannot be found, a retention period has already expired, or a freedom-of-information request arrives for correspondence nobody remembers keeping. Our half-day briefing for administrative staff covers the practical basics that most offices assume everyone already knows but few were ever actually taught: how to classify a document consistently, when a draft becomes a record that must be retained, and which categories of correspondence carry legal retention periods that cannot simply be shortened for convenience.

Participants review real (anonymised) examples of misfiled or prematurely destroyed records and discuss what should have happened instead. A central message of the briefing is that good records management is not primarily about storage space, but about being able to reconstruct, years later, who decided what and on what basis — a requirement that becomes far more visible during an audit or a legal dispute than during ordinary daily work, by which point it is too late to fix retroactively.

items.q: The announcement was met with a mixture of relief and ____.
items.e: „scepticism“ = Skepsis.

items.q: The policy has come under increasing ____ in recent months.
items.e: „to come under scrutiny“ = genau geprüft/unter die Lupe genommen werden.

items.q: The committee's findings were ____ by independent experts before publication.
items.e: „to review findings“ = Ergebnisse überprüfen.

items.q: The country has ____ (pledge) to phase out coal-fired power stations by 2030.
items.e: Present Perfect: „has" + **Partizip II** — „has pledged". Die drei anderen Optionen scheiden aus: „pledge" = Grundform (Infinitiv) — kann in dieser Position nicht stehen; „pledging" = Partizip Präsens — ergäbe eine Verlaufsform, die der Satz nicht verlangt; „pledges" = finite Präsensform der 3. Person Singular — nach einem Hilfsverb ausgeschlossen.

items.q: Scientists have long ____ (warn) that the region is vulnerable to rising sea levels.
items.e: Verlangt ist „warned" — Past Simple von „warn". Die übrigen Optionen sind Formen desselben Verbs, passen aber nicht in die Zeit-/Diathesenlogik des Satzes (warn, warns, warning).

items.q: The new regulation is ____ (design) to curb the misuse of personal data.
items.e: Passiv- bzw. Zustandskonstruktion: „is" + **Partizip II** — „is designed". Person Singular — nach einem Hilfsverb ausgeschlossen; „designing" = Partizip Präsens — ergäbe eine Verlaufsform, die der Satz nicht verlangt.

items.q: The firm was ____ (fine) for failing to implement adequate safeguards.
items.e: Passiv (Präteritum): „was" + **Partizip II** — „was fined". items.q: Health authorities have ____ (launch) a nationwide vaccination campaign.

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „We have followed this policy for 2018.“

We have followed this policy during 2018.
We have followed this policy since 2018.
We have followed this policy from 2018.
items.e: Ein genanntes Jahr als Startpunkt verlangt "since": "since 2018".

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „We can't do nothing until the budget is approved.“
o: We do nothing not until the budget is approved.
We can't did nothing until the budget is approved.
We can't do none until the budget is approved.
We can't do anything until the budget is approved.
items.e: Keine doppelte Verneinung: "can't do anything".

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „Where were the boy which you were looking at?“
o: Where was the boy which you were looking at?
Where was the boy whom you were looking at for?
Where were the boy who you were looking for?
Where was the boy who you were looking for?
items.e: "boy" ist Einzahl → "was"; für Personen "who", nicht "which"; "look for somebody" (jemanden suchen), nicht "look at" hier.

items.q: Identify the correct version of: „The company specialises on renewable energy solutions.“

The company specialises on renewable energies solutions.
The company specialises in renewable energy solutions.
The company specialise in renewable energy solutions.
items.e: "to specialise in something" ist die feste Präposition, nicht "specialise on".

items.q: The certificate issued is valid indefinitely, with no need for renewal.
items.e: Nicht richtig – Text sagt das Gegenteil: „valid for two years, after which a refresher is required“.
items.passage:
Handling personal data responsibly is both a legal obligation and a matter of trust. This course explains, in plain language, the core principles that apply whenever staff collect, store or share personal information: data must be gathered for a specific purpose, kept no longer than necessary, and protected against unauthorised access.

Case studies illustrate common mistakes, such as sending documents to the wrong recipient or storing files on unencrypted personal devices. Participants also learn how to respond if a data breach is suspected, including whom to inform and within what timeframe. The course closes with a short assessment; those who pass receive a certificate valid for two years, after which a refresher is required.

items.q: The workshop focuses mainly on building-access forms and IT accounts.
items.e: Text sagt das Gegenteil: es bewegt sich weg von dieser generischen Checkliste hin zu einem strukturierten Plan.
items.passage:
A new hire's first two weeks shape how long they stay far more than most managers realise. Our one-day workshop for team leads moves induction planning away from a generic checklist of building-access forms and IT accounts towards a structured first-month plan: a clear first task that is genuinely useful rather than symbolic, a named colleague responsible for informal questions the new hire will not want to raise with their manager, and a short check-in at the end of week one specifically to ask what is still unclear, since new hires consistently under-report confusion unless asked directly and repeatedly.

Participants examine anonymised exit-interview data showing that early disengagement is disproportionately linked not to the job itself but to a mismatch between what was promised at interview stage and what the role actually involves in its first weeks. The workshop closes with a session on writing role descriptions that are honest about the less glamorous parts of a job, on the basis that a slightly less appealing but accurate description outperforms an inflated one in the long run.

items.q: The simulated phishing exercise runs after the training, not before.
items.e: Text sagt das Gegenteil: die Übung läuft „before the training rather than after“.
items.passage:
Phishing-awareness training has a credibility problem: staff who have sat through the same slide deck every year tend to click through it on autopilot, which defeats the purpose. Our half-day briefing takes a different approach, running a live simulated phishing exercise before the training rather than after, so participants encounter the material with genuine curiosity about how they personally performed.

The debrief avoids naming individuals but shows aggregated patterns — which pretexts worked best, which department was most susceptible, how much faster people clicked when the message claimed urgency. Participants then work through the specific tells that distinguish a well-crafted phishing attempt from a routine internal email: a request that bypasses the normal approval channel, a sender address that is almost but not quite correct, and pressure to act before verifying through a second channel. The briefing is explicit that the goal is not to make staff paranoid about every email, but to build a habit of pausing on the small number of messages that combine urgency with a request for money, credentials or sensitive data.

items.q: Identifying, assessing, responding to and monitoring risks are the four steps.
items.e: Richtig – Text: „identifying risks, assessing...deciding on a response, and monitoring the risk“.
items.passage:
No plan survives contact with reality unchanged, which is why systematic risk management matters as much for a small project as for an entire organisation. This one-day seminar introduces a simple four-step process: identifying risks, assessing their likelihood and potential impact, deciding on a response, and monitoring the risk throughout the project.

Participants practise the process using realistic scenarios drawn from logistics, IT and public administration. A recurring theme of the seminar is that risks should be owned by a named person, not left as a vague shared responsibility, and that a risk register is only useful if it is reviewed regularly rather than filed away after being created.

items.q: The workshop treats silence from a colleague as reliably meaning disengagement.
items.e: Text sagt das Gegenteil: Kollegen nehmen das oft fälschlich an — „assume silence means disengagement rather than a different working pattern“.
items.passage:
Leading a team spread across four time zones sounds like a scheduling problem until it becomes a trust problem: colleagues who never share a physical room tend to assume silence means disengagement rather than a different working pattern. Our one-day workshop for managers of distributed teams focuses on the habits that substitute for the informal cues lost when a team is not co-located — a short written status update that says what changed since yesterday rather than what someone is generally working on, a norm of responding to urgent messages within an agreed window regardless of local time, and deliberately over-communicating decisions that would otherwise travel by corridor conversation in a single office.

Participants examine case studies of distributed teams that quietly fractured into regional cliques, each assuming the other side understood context that was never actually written down. The workshop closes with a practical session on running a meeting that genuinely includes participants joining at inconvenient local hours, rather than treating their attendance as a courtesy nobody expects to be substantive.

items.passage:
Executive coaching offers senior staff a confidential space to reflect on challenges that are difficult to discuss openly within their own organisation. Unlike training, which teaches skills to a group, coaching is a one-to-one process tailored to the individual's specific situation, typically delivered over six to eight sessions across several months.

A coach does not give direct advice on what decision to make; instead, the coach asks questions that help the client clarify their own thinking, examine blind spots and consider options they may not have considered. Confidentiality is central to the process: coaches do not report the content of sessions to the client's employer, only, where agreed in advance, a brief summary of overall progress.

items.q: The course recommends sampling only the households nearest the main road.
items.e: Text sagt ausdrücklich das Gegenteil: man soll „deliberately reach beyond the accessible edge“, nicht nur die leicht erreichbaren Haushalte.
items.passage:
A humanitarian needs assessment conducted under time pressure risks reflecting whoever was easiest to reach rather than who is actually worst affected. Our two-day methodology course trains field staff to design a sampling approach that deliberately reaches beyond the accessible edge of a crisis zone — the households near the main road, the camp closest to the field office — towards a more representative picture, even when that means additional security clearance and travel time.

Participants practise structured household interviews alongside rapid market assessments, learning to cross-check self-reported need against observable indicators, since respondents sometimes overstate need for strategic reasons and sometimes understate it out of pride or distrust of unfamiliar interviewers. A recurring theme is the danger of a needs assessment that quietly becomes a needs confirmation, reproducing whatever the response plan already assumed rather than testing it. The course ends with a session on writing assessment reports that clearly separate observed data from the assessor's own interpretation, since donors and coordinating agencies need to know which is which.

Unresolved conflict between colleagues rarely disappears on its own; left alone, it tends to escalate and to affect the wider team. This training gives managers and HR staff practical tools to mediate disputes before they reach that point.

Participants learn to separate the emotional and factual layers of a conflict, to conduct a structured mediation conversation in which each side is heard without interruption, and to help parties move from fixed positions towards a workable agreement. items.q: Neutrality is presented as a default state that does not require practice.
items.e: Text sagt ausdrücklich das Gegenteil: „neutrality is a skill, not a default state, and it erodes quickly under pressure“.
items.passage:
Election observers are trained to be neutral, but neutrality is a skill, not a default state, and it erodes quickly under pressure from local contacts eager for a sympathetic reading of events. Our two-day preparation seminar for short-term observers focuses on the practical discipline of observation: recording what was directly witnessed rather than what was reported second-hand, distinguishing an irregularity from a violation, and resisting the pull to draw a conclusion about the whole election from a single, vivid incident at one polling station.

Participants review real observer reports and identify passages where opinion has crept into what should be a factual account. Considerable time is spent on the specific temptation of confirmation bias: observers who arrive expecting problems tend to notice ambiguous incidents that fit that expectation and overlook equally ambiguous ones that do not. The seminar closes with a briefing on personal security procedures and on the strict rule that observers do not intervene directly in polling-station procedures, however tempting that may be in the moment.

items.passage:
Diplomatic and official events follow conventions that, while sometimes appearing formal or old-fashioned, exist to avoid misunderstandings and to show appropriate respect. This course prepares staff who represent their institution at receptions, state visits or official dinners for the practical questions of protocol: correct forms of address, seating order according to rank, and appropriate dress for different occasions.

items.q: The training treats a calm, coherent narrative as always more credible than a distressed one.
items.e: Text warnt ausdrücklich vor diesem „common error“.
items.passage:
Determining whether someone qualifies for refugee status is, in practice, an exercise in weighing credibility under conditions where corroborating evidence is often unavailable by the nature of the claim itself. Our two-day training for caseworkers focuses on structured credibility assessment: distinguishing an inconsistency that undermines a claim from one that is explainable by trauma, memory, translation or the simple passage of time, and avoiding the common error of treating a calm, coherent narrative as inherently more credible than a distressed or fragmented one.

Participants work through anonymised case files, practising interview techniques that allow an applicant to explain apparent contradictions before those contradictions are treated as decisive. A significant part of the training addresses country-of-origin information: how to weigh it against an individual's specific account rather than substituting general conditions for an individualised assessment. The training closes with a session on writing decisions that clearly show the reasoning behind a conclusion, since a poorly reasoned decision undermines confidence in the process even when the underlying conclusion was correct.

items.q: The merger is expected to ____ significant cost savings within two years.

items.q: Participants are ____ (encourage) to try out new behaviours between sessions.
items.e: Passiv- bzw. Zustandskonstruktion: „are" + **Partizip II** — „are encouraged". Die drei anderen Optionen scheiden aus: „encourage" = Grundform (Infinitiv) — kann in dieser Position nicht stehen; „encourages" = finite Präsensform der 3. Person Singular — nach einem Hilfsverb ausgeschlossen; „encouraging" = Partizip Präsens — ergäbe eine Verlaufsform, die der Satz nicht verlangt.

items.q: The workshop has ____ (help) hundreds of managers improve their negotiation skills.
items.e: Present Perfect: „has" + **Partizip II** — „has helped". Die drei anderen Optionen scheiden aus: „helping" = Partizip Präsens — ergäbe eine Verlaufsform, die der Satz nicht verlangt; „help" = Grundform (Infinitiv) — kann in dieser Position nicht stehen; „helps" = finite Präsensform der 3. Person Singular — nach einem Hilfsverb ausgeschlossen; „require" = Grundform (Infinitiv) — kann in dieser Position nicht stehen.

items.q: The trainers have ____ (design) the course around realistic case studies.
items.e: Present Perfect: „have" + **Partizip II** — „have designed". Die drei anderen Optionen scheiden aus: „designs" = finite Präsensform der 3. items.q: New recruits must ____ (undergo) a probationary period before their contract is confirmed.

items.e: Bei zwei Alternativen Komparativ mit Artikel („the less costly", „the quicker"); „lesser" ist ein Adjektiv, kein Steigerungswort vor Adjektiven.

items.q: The seminar claims digital transformation is simply about introducing new software.
items.e: Nicht richtig – Text sagt das Gegenteil: „often misunderstood as simply introducing new software“.
items.passage:
Digital transformation is often misunderstood as simply introducing new software, when in fact the greater challenge lies in changing working habits and decision-making processes. This seminar helps non-technical managers understand the opportunities and limits of automation, data analysis and digital collaboration tools, without requiring any programming knowledge.

Case studies show how organisations have used digital tools to speed up routine approvals, to make decisions based on real data rather than assumption, and, in some cases, to fail expensively by digitising a broken process instead of first fixing it. Participants leave with a simple framework for judging whether a proposed digital initiative addresses a genuine problem or merely follows a passing trend.

items.q: The briefing assumes a filed evacuation plan is sufficient on its own.
items.e: Text sagt ausdrücklich das Gegenteil: es geht um die Lücke zwischen einem Plan auf Papier und einem, der wirklich funktioniert.
items.passage:
Duty-of-care obligations for staff posted overseas extend well beyond having an evacuation plan filed somewhere in a folder. Our one-day briefing for security focal points works through the gap between a plan that exists on paper and one that would actually function under pressure: whether staff know the assembly point without checking a document, whether contact trees have been tested in the last six months rather than merely updated, and whether the plan accounts for staff who are travelling, on leave, or living outside the main compound at the moment a crisis begins.

Participants run a tabletop exercise simulating a rapidly deteriorating security situation, discovering in real time which assumptions in their own plan do not survive contact with a plausible scenario. A recurring finding from past sessions is that plans fail less often because of missing information than because of unclear decision authority — nobody is quite sure who is empowered to trigger an evacuation before headquarters can be reached. The briefing ends with a session on documenting decisions taken under time pressure, for review after the fact.

items.q: The training covers how to measure an organisation's environmental footprint.
items.e: Richtig – Text: „how to measure an organisation's environmental footprint“.
items.passage:
Environmental responsibility has moved from a marginal concern to a central factor in how organisations are judged by partners, regulators and the public. This training equips staff with a practical understanding of how to measure an organisation's environmental footprint, set realistic reduction targets, and report progress credibly, without falling into the trap of exaggerated claims that cannot be substantiated.

Participants examine case studies of both successful sustainability programmes and instances of so-called greenwashing, where public claims went well beyond actual practice. A practical exercise asks small groups to draft a simple, honest sustainability statement for a fictional organisation, based only on the data provided, and to defend it against sceptical questioning from the trainers.

items.q: The briefing focuses on physically guarding a single famous site.
items.e: Text sagt das Gegenteil: es geht meist um Dokumentation, rechtliche Kennzeichnung und Koordination, nicht primär um physische Bewachung.
items.passage:
Protecting cultural heritage during armed conflict is rarely a matter of physically guarding a single famous site; more often it is a question of documentation, legal marking and rapid coordination before damage becomes irreversible. Our one-day briefing for field staff covers the practical basics: how to identify and photograph at-risk sites and collections before a situation deteriorates further, the meaning and limits of the distinctive emblem used to mark protected cultural property under international law, and the channels through which looted or illegally exported objects can be reported to increase the chance of eventual recovery.

Participants examine case studies where advance documentation later proved decisive in establishing that an object had in fact been looted, since without a pre-existing photographic record and provenance file, claims are far harder to substantiate after the fact. The briefing is explicit that protecting heritage is not a substitute for protecting people, but a parallel obligation that competes for the same limited attention and resources during a crisis, which is precisely why advance preparation matters more than improvisation in the moment.

items.q: An initial holding statement acknowledges the situation without speculation.
items.e: Richtig – Text: „acknowledges the situation and commits to further information without speculating“.
items.passage:
In the first hours of a crisis, silence is often mistaken for guilt, even when an organisation is still establishing the facts. This training prepares communication teams to respond quickly and responsibly when something goes seriously wrong, whether an accident, a data breach or a public controversy.

Participants practise drafting an initial holding statement, which acknowledges the situation and commits to further information without speculating on causes before they are known. The course also covers coordinating a single, consistent message across departments, so that spokespeople do not contradict one another, and monitoring social media for rumours that may need to be addressed directly. A full-day simulation puts participants through a realistic, fast-moving crisis scenario.

items.q: The course treats open-source analysis as simply reading more news than colleagues.
items.e: Text sagt ausdrücklich das Gegenteil: das „undersells both the discipline and the risk involved“.
items.passage:
Open-source intelligence analysis is often mistaken for simply reading more news than one's colleagues, which undersells both the discipline and the risk involved. Our two-day course trains analysts to systematically evaluate a source before relying on it: who benefits from the claim being believed, whether the same image or video has been recycled from an earlier, unrelated event, and whether a claim has been independently corroborated or merely repeated across outlets that all cite the same original, unverified post.

Participants practise reverse image searches and geolocation techniques on real (historical) case material, learning how small visual details — shadow angles, vegetation, signage in an unfamiliar script — can confirm or rule out a claimed location. A significant part of the course addresses the analyst's own confirmation bias: the tendency to scrutinise sources that contradict an emerging hypothesis far more critically than sources that support it. The course closes with guidance on assigning and communicating confidence levels honestly, rather than presenting a probable inference with the same certainty as a confirmed fact.

items.q: The course is designed for non-financial managers.
items.e: Richtig – Text: „designed for non-financial managers“.
items.passage:
Many capable managers make sound operational decisions yet feel uneasy reading a balance sheet or a profit-and-loss statement. This course is designed for non-financial managers who need to understand the numbers behind their department without becoming accountants.

Participants learn to read the three core financial statements, to understand the difference between profit and cash flow, and to see how their own decisions, such as delaying a purchase or extending payment terms to a client, affect the wider financial picture. Practical exercises use simplified, realistic figures rather than abstract theory, and participants finish the course able to ask informed questions in a budget meeting rather than nodding along without understanding the details.

items.q: The briefing treats all gifts above a threshold as automatically corrupt.
items.e: Text sagt das Gegenteil: „most gifts are entirely innocent“; die Regeln dienen einem anderen Zweck.
items.passage:
Diplomatic gift protocol looks like a minor courtesy question until it collides with conflict-of-interest rules that were written for a very different context. Our half-day briefing for protocol officers works through the practical grey zones: gifts received in a purely ceremonial capacity versus those linked to a specific pending decision, the declining monetary thresholds above which a gift must be formally logged rather than simply accepted with thanks, and the awkward but necessary conversation about redirecting an inappropriate gift to an official collection rather than a personal residence.

Participants review anonymised real cases, including one where a modest gift became reportable only because of unfortunate timing relative to an unrelated procurement decision. The briefing stresses that the rules exist less to prevent any individual instance of corruption — most gifts are entirely innocent — than to protect the recipient from a later, unfounded accusation that could otherwise be impossible to disprove once the moment has passed and no record exists.

items.q: The course assumes the risks discussed most during negotiation are the ones that later materialise.
items.e: Text sagt ausdrücklich das Gegenteil: „the risks that actually materialise are rarely the ones both sides spent the most time discussing“.
items.passage:
Negotiating a public-private partnership contract is as much about anticipating the years after signature as about the signature itself, since the risks that actually materialise are rarely the ones both sides spent the most time discussing. Our two-day course for government negotiators focuses on risk allocation clauses that are easy to draft vaguely and expensive to interpret later: which party bears the cost of a regulatory change during the contract term, what happens if projected usage figures — for a toll road or a utility, say — fall persistently short of forecast, and how a dispute resolution mechanism actually performs once both sides have genuinely diverging interests rather than a shared goal of reaching agreement.

Participants negotiate a simulated contract against a private-sector counterpart played by course facilitators, then compare their draft clauses against clauses from real contracts that later required renegotiation, identifying precisely where the original ambiguity originated. A closing session addresses the temptation to treat a lower headline price as automatically better value, when long-term liability exposure may make it considerably more expensive overall.

items.q: The course covers drafting notes verbales and briefing notes.
items.e: Richtig – Text: „trains staff to draft notes verbales, briefing notes and formal letters“.
items.passage:
Written diplomatic communication follows conventions that differ noticeably from ordinary business correspondence, both in tone and in structure. This course trains staff to draft notes verbales, briefing notes and formal letters that are precise, appropriately restrained in tone, and unambiguous even when addressing sensitive matters.

Participants practise structuring a briefing note so that the most important recommendation appears first, followed by supporting analysis, rather than building up to a conclusion at the end. Careful attention is given to register: diplomatic language often expresses disagreement through understatement rather than direct criticism, and participants learn to recognise, and to produce, such phrasing appropriately. The course also covers the correct handling of confidentiality markings and distribution lists.

items.q: Risk reduction and disaster response are treated as asking the same question.
items.e: Text sagt ausdrücklich das Gegenteil: „the two ask fundamentally different questions“.
items.passage:
Disaster-risk-reduction planning is frequently confused with disaster response planning, even though the two ask fundamentally different questions: response asks how to act once an event has begun, while risk reduction asks how to make the event less likely, or its impact smaller, before it ever occurs. Our two-day planning course for municipal and regional officials works through hazard mapping, the practical difference between a hazard and a vulnerability, and the specific trap of investing heavily in the most recent past disaster while remaining under-prepared for a different, plausible hazard that simply has not occurred yet in living memory.

Participants build a simplified risk-reduction plan for a fictional municipality, prioritising interventions not by which hazard feels most vivid but by an explicit calculation combining likelihood, potential impact and the cost of mitigation. A recurring theme is the political difficulty of funding prevention, since a disaster that is successfully prevented produces no visible event to justify the spending that prevented it, unlike response spending after a disaster that has already happened.

items.q: Tariffs and non-tariff barriers are distinguished in the course.
items.e: Richtig – Text: „the difference between tariffs and non-tariff barriers“.
items.passage:
Cross-border trade involves a web of rules that can trap the unwary, from customs classification to export controls on sensitive goods. This course gives non-lawyers a working understanding of the key legal concepts involved in international trade, including the difference between tariffs and non-tariff barriers, the basic structure of trade agreements, and the compliance obligations that arise when exporting controlled technology.

Case studies illustrate the consequences of misclassifying goods or overlooking a licensing requirement, including significant fines and reputational damage. The course does not train participants to replace legal counsel, but to recognise situations that require it, and to ask legal or compliance colleagues the right questions early, before a shipment is already in transit.

items.q: A formal handover note is said to reliably capture the knowledge that is hardest to replace.
items.e: Text sagt das Gegenteil: es erfasst eher, „what is easy to write down rather than what is actually hard to replace“.
items.passage:
Institutional knowledge walks out the door with a departing staff member far more often than handover procedures are designed to prevent, since a formal handover note is usually written under time pressure and captures what is easy to write down rather than what is actually hard to replace. Our one-day workshop for outgoing and incoming post-holders focuses on surfacing the second kind of knowledge: which stakeholder relationships depend on informal trust built over years, which recurring problems have an unwritten workaround that nobody thought worth documenting because it seemed obvious, and which files look complete but are missing the context needed to understand why a past decision was actually made.

Participants practise a structured handover interview technique, asking the departing staff member what they would want to know on their own first day if they were starting the role fresh. A recurring finding is that the most valuable handover content is rarely produced by asking a general question like "is there anything I should know", but by asking about specific recent situations and working backwards from there.

A recurring finding is that the most valuable handover content is rarely produced by asking a general question like "is there anything I should know", but by asking about specific recent situations and working backwards from there.

items.q: The deciding factor for whistleblowers is mainly the exact wording of the policy.
items.e: Text sagt ausdrücklich das Gegenteil: entscheidend ist, ob frühere Fälle sichtbar geschützt wurden, nicht der Wortlaut.
items.passage:
Whistleblower protection policies are frequently well drafted on paper and poorly trusted in practice, since the deciding factor for a potential whistleblower is rarely the wording of the policy but whether colleagues who spoke up in the past were visibly protected or quietly sidelined. Our half-day briefing for managers examines the practical mechanics of a credible internal reporting channel: guaranteeing that a report can be made without going through the reporter's own direct manager, who may be implicated; setting realistic expectations about how long an investigation actually takes, since vague promises of speed erode trust when they are not met; and training managers specifically on the retaliation that is hardest to prove — a subtle change in tone, being quietly excluded from meetings, projects reassigned without explanation.

Participants discuss anonymised past cases where retaliation was never formally admitted but was nonetheless unmistakable to everyone involved. The briefing closes by stressing that a policy is only as credible as the most recent case colleagues actually witnessed.

items.q: Consular staff are described as the first point of contact for citizens in difficulty abroad.
items.e: Richtig – Text: „often the first point of contact for citizens facing the most difficult moments...abroad“.
items.passage:
Consular staff are often the first point of contact for citizens facing the most difficult moments of their lives abroad, from lost documents to serious accidents or arrest. This training prepares new consular officers for the practical and emotional demands of the role.

Participants practise handling distressed callers with empathy while gathering the precise information needed to act, and learn the procedures for emergency passports, next-of-kin notification, and liaison with local authorities and hospitals. The course stresses the limits of consular assistance: officers can offer support and advocate for fair treatment, but cannot interfere in another state's legal proceedings or guarantee a particular outcome. Self-care for staff who regularly handle distressing cases is also addressed.

items.q: A treaty's provisions are said to take effect domestically immediately upon signature.
items.e: Text sagt ausdrücklich das Gegenteil: die meisten Verträge benötigen erst Umsetzungsgesetzgebung.
items.passage:
A treaty's signature is only the beginning of the work that determines whether it actually changes anything domestically, since most treaties require implementing legislation before their provisions have any effect within national law. Our two-day course for legal officers covers the practical steps of transposition: identifying which existing domestic laws must be amended rather than simply supplemented, spotting provisions that are self-executing versus those that explicitly require further domestic legislative action, and managing the frequent gap between the timeline a treaty anticipates for implementation and the actual pace of a domestic legislative calendar.

Participants work through a simplified transposition exercise for a fictional treaty, drafting the amendments a national parliament would need to pass and flagging provisions likely to face domestic legal or constitutional obstacles. A recurring theme of the course is that a state can be in good-faith breach of a treaty simply through legislative delay, without ever having intended non-compliance, which is precisely why early identification of transposition obstacles matters more than most ratification debates suggest.

items.q: The course focuses only on the professional content of the new role.
items.e: Nicht richtig – Text sagt das Gegenteil: Mitarbeiter „underestimate the everyday business customs“, der Kurs füllt genau diese Lücke.
items.passage:
Staff taking up a posting abroad often prepare thoroughly for the professional content of their new role, yet underestimate the everyday business customs that can make or break early working relationships. This short course prepares participants for practical situations such as exchanging business cards, addressing colleagues correctly, structuring meetings, and interpreting silence or indirect answers, which can carry very different meanings from one culture to another.

Rather than presenting a long list of dos and don'ts for every country, the course teaches a small number of underlying principles, such as observing before acting and asking a trusted local colleague when in doubt. Participants also discuss how to handle situations in which local practice conflicts with their organisation's own compliance rules.

items.q: Fraud detection is presented mainly as spotting an obviously forged document.
items.e: Text sagt ausdrücklich das Gegenteil: es geht eher um Muster, die erst über viele Anträge hinweg sichtbar werden.
items.passage:
Detecting visa and consular fraud is less often a matter of spotting an obviously forged document than of noticing a pattern that only becomes visible across many applications rather than within a single one. Our two-day training for consular officers covers document examination basics, but places equal weight on behavioural and pattern-based indicators: near-identical supporting documents submitted by applicants who claim no connection to one another, a sudden cluster of applications routed through the same facilitator shortly after that facilitator's usual channel was closed elsewhere, and interview answers that are technically consistent with each other but suspiciously rehearsed in phrasing.

Participants review anonymised case files where fraud was ultimately established, working backwards to identify which early indicator, visible at the time, was initially dismissed as coincidence. The training is explicit that most applicants are entirely genuine, and that officers who treat every applicant with generalised suspicion both cause unnecessary hardship and, paradoxically, become less effective at noticing the specific patterns that actually indicate fraud.

The training is explicit that most applicants are entirely genuine, and that officers who treat every applicant with generalised suspicion both cause unnecessary hardship and, paradoxically, become less effective at noticing the specific patterns that actually indicate fraud.

items.q: The course claims pressure can never sharpen performance.
items.e: Nicht richtig – Text sagt das Gegenteil: „A certain amount of pressure can sharpen performance“.
items.passage:
A certain amount of pressure can sharpen performance, but sustained stress without recovery eventually undermines health, judgement and working relationships. This training helps staff in demanding roles recognise the early warning signs of chronic stress in themselves and in colleagues, before these develop into burnout.

Participants learn practical techniques for regulating their response under pressure, including structured breathing exercises and brief attention resets between demanding tasks, as well as longer-term habits such as protecting recovery time and setting realistic boundaries around availability outside working hours. The course explicitly does not treat resilience as simply enduring more pressure silently; instead, it frames resilience as the ability to recover well and to seek support early, before a crisis develops.

items.q: Incoming chairs are assumed to already be familiar with procedural precedents.
items.e: Text sagt das Gegenteil: sie kommen oft „with limited familiarity with the specific procedural precedents“.
items.passage:
An organisation with a rotating chairperson risks losing institutional continuity precisely at the moments it can least afford to, since incoming chairs often arrive with genuine expertise in their field but limited familiarity with the specific procedural precedents that govern how the body actually operates. Our one-day briefing for incoming chairs and their support staff works through the practical mechanics of a good succession: a structured handover briefing that goes beyond a formal welcome to cover unresolved procedural disputes still simmering from the previous term, a clear record of which precedents were set informally rather than through a written rule, and early identification of which agenda items were deliberately deferred rather than genuinely resolved.

Participants review a case study of a body that reopened a long-settled procedural question simply because the new chair was unaware it had already been settled, consuming a full session that could have been spent on substance. The briefing closes by stressing that continuity does not mean an incoming chair cannot change direction, only that any change should be a deliberate choice rather than an accidental one.
